extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical rhetoric and prose style, translators, and writers interested in classical principles of prose
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging Greek (and analogously modern) prose, derived from Demetrius' De elocutione: classifications of style, structural rules (members/periods), rhetorical devices, and aesthetic principles for clarity, rhythm, and appropriateness of diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Four Types of Style
rubrics_metrics.description: The four types of style (yapaxripes ris eppnvelas) are: the plain (icyvds), the elevated (veyadorperys), the elegant (yAadupés), the forcible (Sevvds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each type is treated as a distinct dimension of prose; Demetrius analyzes them in order (plain, elevated, elegant, forcible) and discusses how to achieve or avoid each. Use this fourfold classification as a primary rubric for diagnosing tone and mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevated Style (peyarorperis) — three loci
rubrics_metrics.description: Elevation in composition or arrangement (atvOerrs peyarorperis); elevation in subject matter (tpaypata peyadorperns); elevation in diction (AEfus peyadorperijs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for the elevated style, attend to structure (arrangement of members/periods), the grandeur of subject matter (a great theme is necessary to the grand style), and dignified diction. All three loci contribute to elevation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frigidity as the correlative vice of elevation
rubrics_metrics.description: Frigidity (Wvxpov) is the correlative vice of the elevated style and arises at three points: dudvou, AEkis, atvOerrs; its acme is reached in hyperbole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overwrought expression, hyperbole, and cold, lifeless elevation. Recognize that attempts at elevation can produce frigidity if applied injudiciously to subject, diction, or composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject must create the style
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject must create the style—that a great theme is necessary to the grand style, which otherwise will be merely grandiose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match stylistic loftiness to genuinely substantial subject matter; do not use elevated diction for trivial or base topics (no beauty of language can ennoble what is essentially base).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bombast, bathos, preciosity, and affectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Bombast and bathos are among the faults ridiculed, together with preciosity and affectations of all sorts; style has the defects of its qualities and the greater the height attempted the greater the fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for excessive ornament, forced grandiosity, or preciousness of phrase; these are anti-patterns demonstrating poor judgment in style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lucidity (clarity) of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Demetrius praises lucidity and explains obscurity (e.g., Heracleitus' language) as a fault to be recognized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor clear expression that communicates ideas; evaluate prose for how readily a reader can follow and comprehend the argument or narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose rhythm (prose mesurée) and sentence shape
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a rhythm (a prose mesurée) which pays special heed to the beginning and the end of sentences; 'measure' in prose is necessary—prose must not sprawl illimitably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to cadence and balance at sentence openings and closings; craft periods with attention to rhythmic effect analogous to meter in verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety in sentence/clause length and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognizes the need of variety—of intermingling shorter with longer clauses or sentences, and of passing from one type of style to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate lengths and structures to maintain reader interest and to shape emphasis; monotony of uniformly long or short clauses is a fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of words with noble associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Many niceties in Greek prose-writing such as the choice of words with noble associations are important for fine style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select diction whose connotations suit the intended tone; prefer words carrying suitable cultural or literary associations for elevated effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proverbs 'in season' and in letter-writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Proverbs are valued when used in season; in §232: 'it is the wisdom of a people, it is the wisdom of the world.' Their frequent use in letter-writing is recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ familiar sayings judiciously to connect with readers' common wisdom; particularly effective in epistolary contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage-language for audience engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of stage-language—one in which the actor finds it easy to make us think with him and feel with him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, adopt a performative register that helps elicit audience empathy and shared perspective, but avoid theatrical excess if the subject demands restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antithesis: use sparingly and with care
rubrics_metrics.description: Antithesis can be overdone and seem like false artifice; though a useful device, it may be excessive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrast and balanced opposition to rhetorical effect, but avoid mechanical or repeated antithesis that reads as contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of expression and thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Demetrius is apt to busy himself with the expression of thought to the partial neglect of thought itself; Aristotle focuses more on subject-matter than on language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that stylistic flourish does not supplant intellectual substance; assess both idea-quality and linguistic execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose should avoid both artifice and negligence
rubrics_metrics.description: All good prose is, as he assumes, the offspring neither of artifice nor negligence but (like poetry) of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for crafted naturalness—skillful form that does not call attention to itself as contrived or slipshod.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic vs disjointed styles; period types
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes the periodic and the disjointed style (epunveia kaTertpapmevn, epunveta Sunpnpevn); identifies types of period: narrative period, rhetorical period, conversational period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose structural mode (periodic vs disjointed) appropriate to rhetorical purpose; evaluate number and arrangement of 'members' in a period for balance and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Members (kolon), phrases, and structural cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of 'members' (x@Aov), the 'phrase' (koupa), the period (zepiodos); includes topics like symmetrical members, members with similar terminations (6povotéXevta) and cautions regarding their use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose periods from well-defined members; avoid repetitive or mechanically similar endings that produce monotony or ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enthymeme versus period
rubrics_metrics.description: Difference between the enthymeme (év@ipunya) and the period is treated; the enthymeme is distinct from the period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing argumentative prose, distinguish logical argument structure (enthymeme) from periodical sentence construction; don't conflate rhetorical reasoning with syntactic periodicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures of speech and their regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections on figures of speech (cyjpara éEews) and special topics such as hiatus (otyxpovors dovnevTwv).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhetorical figures thoughtfully; monitor phonetic and metrical effects such as hiatus that may jar the ear; annotate examples from models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter-writing: definition and brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition of a letter as 'the heart's good wishes in brief.' Sections §223-235 on the art of letter-writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For epistolary prose prioritize sincerity and concision; letters should be compact expressions of goodwill and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave much unsaid—reader participation
rubrics_metrics.description: With Theophrastus, Demetrius sees that distinction comes to style no less through what is not said than through what is said: much should be left to the reader's own perception and imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use implication and omission to engage the reader's inferential work rather than over-explaining; value suggestiveness and restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core positive qualities (Xapaktip toxvos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demetrius groups some of the best qualities of style under Xapaktip toxvos: clearness, vividness, naturalness, persuasiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four positive qualities as a checklist when composing or judging prose: prioritize clarity, vivid imagery, natural expression, and convincing argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling on great authors; borrowing 'Greek ears' and taste
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to carry readers back to the great writers of Greece; these critics give the stimulus of an added appreciation and enjoyment—'we are borrowing Greek ears and Greek taste.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study exemplary texts (Homer, Plato, Demosthenes, Sappho, etc.) as living models; use illustrative quotations to demonstrate principles in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of editorial revision — avoid repetitions and inconsistencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the weaknesses of Style may be reckoned sundry repetitions, inconsistencies, and digressions—defects partly due to want of revision for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize revision to remove repetition, inconsistency, and unnecessary digression; a polished text reflects editorial care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hyperbole as stylistic excess
rubrics_metrics.description: The very acme of frigidity is reached in hyperbole (124–126): an example of how elevated aims can become a vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat hyperbolic exaggeration skeptically; use restraint to prevent elevation from tipping into parody or bathos.
